The ongoing crisis follows a severe security deterioration across the Arsi Zone. Human rights monitors and the Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church have repeatedly raised alarms regarding systematic attacks targeting rural communities, local clergy, and agrarian populations. Armed groups operating throughout the region have launched repeated incursions involving mass casualty assaults on rural villages, targeted executions, and the destruction of agricultural livelihoods. These attacks have driven widespread civilian flight across multiple woredas, including Merti, Shirka, Aseko, and Robe. Community representatives report that recurring security breaches have completely displaced residents across 21 of the 23 administrative kebeles in Merti Woreda. Only two kebeles in the entire woreda currently maintain active residential populations in their homes. Many affected families have lived in temporary displacement for up to three years after being forced off their ancestral farmlands, while newly displaced victims from late-October attacks face critical survival conditions without official shelter infrastructure. Displaced residents report that victims are currently living in makeshift conditions, relying on informal rental arrangements or host families willing to accommodate them. Displaced women, children, and elderly citizens face acute shortages of food, clothing, and basic medical care, with community members emphasizing that no direct relief aid has reached the majority of victims. Responding to the emergency, Merti Woreda Administrator Ato Abdelkerim Mohamed acknowledged that daily relief assistance—including support coordinated through federal disaster risk structures and the zonal Disaster Prevention and Preparedness Office (BUSAGONOFA)—remains active. However, he admitted that current aid flows are severely insufficient to meet the scale of displacement and called on charitable organizations and international relief agencies to assist affected populations. __ Join our Telegram Channel : t.me/borkena Like borkena on Facebook Ethiopian Sports News Join the conversation. ethiopia.summary: Mass displacement continues in Merti Woreda, Oromia region, due to a severe security breakdown in the Arsi Zone. Hundreds of families have been forced to flee their homes amid ongoing violence, leaving them without permanent shelter or adequate humanitarian aid. Reports indicate that armed groups have conducted systematic attacks on rural communities, leading to mass casualties and the destruction of agricultural livelihoods. As a result, 21 out of 23 administrative kebeles in Merti Woreda are now largely uninhabited, with only two maintaining active populations. Many displaced individuals have been living in temporary conditions for up to three years, facing critical shortages of food, clothing, and medical care. Despite the acknowledgment of ongoing relief efforts by local authorities, the aid provided is insufficient to meet the overwhelming needs of the displaced population. Community leaders are calling for increased support from charitable organizations and international relief agencies to address the humanitarian crisis.

ethiopia.title: Proxy politics and border clashes: an escalating crisis between Sudan and Ethiopia – Ayin network - شبكة عاين
ethiopia.content: Proxy politics and border clashes: an escalating crisis between Sudan and Ethiopia – Ayin network – شبكة عاين Contact Us About Us Donate No videos yet! Click on "Watch later" to add videos here View all videos Home Investigative Reports Videos Advanced Search العربية English Investigative Reports Proxy politics and border clashes: an escalating crisis between Sudan and Ethiopia Ayin Network 17 hours ago 17 hours ago 360 9 November 2026 The diplomatic rift between Sudan and Ethiopia has evolved past border disputes this month, exposing competing geopolitical interests along the Red Sea. Last week, Ethiopian authorities shuttered the Sudanese consulate in Assosa, giving staff 48 hours to evacuate. Khartoum swiftly retaliated, closing the Ethiopian consulate in the eastern city of Gedaref and expelling its diplomatic personnel. This diplomatic severing followed Sudan’s November 1 formal complaint to the United Nations Security Council and the African Union Peace and Security Council. Khartoum accused Addis Ababa of allowing the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to use Ethiopian territory as a staging ground for drone strikes. According to unverified Sudanese government data, the complaint documented 70 attacks involving 187 drones over the past year, resulting in widespread civilian casualties. In response, Addis Ababa categorically denied providing military or logistical support to the Rapid Support Forces. Instead, Ethiopia issued counter-accusations, claiming that Khartoum, Cairo, and Asmara backed Tigrayan fighters who launched an offensive against Ethiopian government forces in September 2026—a charge all three capitals deny. With the Sudanese civil war expanding and conflicts in northern Ethiopia reigniting, the shared border is rapidly becoming a site for regional rivalries. This escalating tension threatens to replace direct military engagement with a debilitating, multi-front proxy war involving the overlapping interests of Egypt, Eritrea, and the United Arab Emirates. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (Social Media) Regional distrust The Sudan-Ethiopia rift cannot be isolated from other rivalries involving Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Egypt. Following the 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement, Ethiopia’s relationship with Eritrea rapidly deteriorated. On October 1, 2026, Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and expelled Eritrean diplomats, prompting Asmara to completely sever diplomatic ties. At the core of this dispute lies the future of the Tigray region and landlocked Ethiopia’s strategic campaign to secure sovereign access to the Red Sea. At the same time, the historical rivalry between Egypt and Ethiopia—rooted in the management of the Nile waters and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD)—has broadened into a struggle over regional security. These intersecting rivalries have fostered what Dereje Fessa, senior research and policy advisor at the Ethiopian Institute for Life, calls a “dangerous dynamic of reciprocity”. Fessa notes that growing Sudanese anxiety over the strategic partnership between Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s administration and the UAE is fuelling military concerns in Khartoum, especially given widespread allegations of Abu Dhabi backing the RSF. However, the distrust is mutual. Fessa points to the historical alliance between the Sudanese military establishment and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) dating back to their shared struggle against the Derg regime in the 1970s and 1980s. This history heavily colours Ethiopia’s current security calculus. “The crossing of elements from Tigray’s “Army 72” into Sudan, their seeking refuge under the protection of the Sudanese army, and their subsequent involvement in military operations to recapture Khartoum raised concerns in Addis Ababa about the possibility of these fighters being rearmed,” Fessa observed. Consequently, Addis Ababa accuses Sudan of becoming a conduit for weapons flowing from Egypt and Eritrea to armed Ethiopian factions, while Khartoum maintains that Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region operates as a logistical hub for the RSF. African affairs researcher Mohamed Torshin notes that alleged supply routes through Assosa have yielded tangible battlefield results, enabling the RSF to capture vital territory in Sudan’s Blue Nile State. Kurmuk bridge construction (Yale HRL) Road construction and repair in Kurmuk (Yale HRL) The Yale Humanitarian Research Lab (HRL) recently identified a significant RSF presence and infrastructure development in Kurmuk, a strategic border city in Sudan’s southern Blue Nile State. Kurmuk sits on a critical artery connecting Al Damazin, Sudan (approximately 140 kilometres north), to Assosa, Ethiopia (85 kilometres south). According to Yale HRL, satellite imagery from October shows the RSF repaired the Kurmuk bridge and roads connecting Sudan to Ethiopia. Analysts suggest that these infrastructure projects aimed to ensure RSF supply lines from the border. TPLF fighters in the current conflict (social media) The proxy war paradigm Shared Sudan-Ethiopia border areas in Benishangul, Gedaref, Al-Fashqa, and now Kurmuk are fertile ground for direct security competition. Khaled Mohamed Taha, a researcher and expert on the Horn of Africa, highlights how regional governments are increasingly leveraging non-state actors to destabilise their neighbours and project power. “The lines between local conflicts and regional wars have blurred. Armed groups on each side have become tools of pressure and strategic balance, complicating the chances of internal political settlement and turning every civil crisis into a bargaining chip in a cross-border regional power game,” Taha stated. Torshin notes that a direct, conventional war between Sudan and Ethiopia remains unlikely due to the prohibitive economic and military costs. Instead, the conflict is solidifying into a proxy war model, pitting the Ethiopian-RSF axis against a loose, pragmatic triad of Khartoum, Cairo, and Asmara. Taha cautions against viewing these axes as rigid alliances, describing them instead as temporary security arrangements driven by overlapping immediate interests. Yet the consequences of this indirect warfare could prove catastrophic, particularly as they intersect with Ethiopia’s pursuit of a Red Sea port and Eritrea’s fierce defence of its sovereignty. “Any military confrontation between Ethiopia and Eritrea, in parallel with the Sudanese war, could draw in South Sudan, Somalia, and Djibouti and threaten the safety of international navigation,” Taha warned. While utilising armed proxies may appear to be a low-cost alternative to direct military engagement for the region’s governments, Taha believes it represents the most destructive long-term trajectory for the Horn of Africa, threatening to permanently erode state sovereignty and societal stability across multiple borders. Recently, Ethiopia closed the Sudanese consulate in Assosa, prompting Sudan to reciprocate by shutting down the Ethiopian consulate in Gedaref. This diplomatic fallout followed Sudan's complaint to the UN and African Union, accusing Ethiopia of allowing the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to launch drone strikes from its territory. somalia.title: British-Somali ‌‌‌‌boxer Ramla Ali defeats Mikiah Kreps for first ⁠⁠⁠⁠world title - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: British-Somali ‌‌‌‌boxer Ramla Ali defeats Mikiah Kreps for first ⁠⁠⁠⁠world title - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS British-Somali ‌‌‌‌boxer Ramla Ali defeats Mikiah Kreps for first ⁠⁠⁠⁠world title Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Andy Richardson Tuesday November 10, 2026 Ali, who fled Somalia’s civil war and settled in London, won the controversial split-decision fight against American Kreps to claim IBO and WBF junior featherweight belts. Ramla Ali, right, fights Mikiah Kreps during the third round of their bout for the vacant IBF and WBO women's junior featherweight world titles on November 8, 2026, in Arlington, Texas [Julio Cortez/AP] Ramla Ali, a British Somali boxer whose life story is the subject of a new film, has realised a long-held dream and won her first world title to claim two vacant junior featherweight belts in the United States. The 36-year-old landed the biggest titles of her career by winning the IBO and WBF belts in a controversial split-decision victory over American fighter Mikiah Kreps in Arlington, Texas, on Sunday. advertisements The nail-biting nature of the 10-round contest should not have come as too much of a surprise, as the duo are former sparring partners and ended the night with an expression of mutual respect. “Mikiah, I want to share this victory with you because you pushed me for 10 rounds,” an emotional Ali said while addressing her opponent, who she stopped from exiting the ring after being declared the winner. “I kept saying I’m so tired because your work rate was next level. I don’t know how I kept up, so thank you for being such a great boxer.” Mikiah Kreps was covered in blood as she fought Ramla Ali [Julio Cortez/AP] The 30-year-old Niagara Falls native reciprocated the emotion. “I respect you,” Kreps said as both fighters wrapped an arm around each other. During the fight, Ali had Kreps on the canvas in round three, but she was behind her younger opponent in the overall punch count at the end of the fight. The outcome of the fight caused controversy from the moment the referee lifted Ali’s arm when the decision was announced. According to the official punch statistics from the fight, Kreps outlanded Ali by 115 blows to 78 and the American was also way ahead in the power shot count. One judge scored the bout 98-91 for Kreps but the other judges saw the fight differently and gave Ali the win with scores of 97-92 and 96-93. Veteran promoter Lou Di Bella wrote on social media, “Mikiah Kreps won that fight and it wasn’t even close. Stevie Wonder could see that.” From Somalia’s civil war to world champion The external noise would have mattered little to Ali, who dropped to her knees when the scores were announced. Ali and her family are no strangers to adversity, having settled in London in 1992 after fleeing Somalia during its civil war. Years after picking up the sport as a teenager in East London, Ali became the first Somali boxer to compete at the Olympic Games when she represented the country of her birth at Tokyo 2020. She later became the first Muslim woman to win an English amateur boxing title. Ali’s journey has provided the inspiration for the movie ‘In the Shadows’ starring Top Boy actor Jasmine Jobson. Ali wept as she dropped to the mat after winning her first world title [Julio Cortez/AP] The fighter lost her father earlier this year and said she stayed up all night prior to the fight, wishing he would have been around to see her in the ring. “My father passed away in May, so I was really emotional,” she said in a post-fight interview with All The Smoke Boxing. “Every round, I kept going to my corner to tell my coach I couldn’t do it any more because I was physically exhausted. I boxed through my skin and I’m glad I got the victory.” Ali’s career has always been multi-dimensional. As a model and UNICEF ambassador, she has projected her voice beyond sporting arenas. “I can’t put into words what this means to me and what this means to all of Somalia,” she said, fighting back tears, while standing inside the ring. “I’ve hopefully inspired so many young girls and boys out there to dream big and that’s all I’ve ever wanted to do.” More News Unlocking Somalia's Investment Potential- Opportunities in the Blue Economy, Fisheries, Energy and Agriculture Guleid Osman Somali president inaugurates new Hirshabelle parliament and security ministry buildings in Jowhar HOL Somali President joins world leaders at COP31 climate summit in Turkey HOL Somali defence minister meets Chinese ambassador after talks with U.S. diplomat HOL U.S. maintains level 4 travel advisories for Uganda, DRC, Somalia and South Sudan Kenyans About HOL Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs Categories Opinion Somali Links Follow Us All Rights Reserved Copyright © 1999-2026, www.hiiraan.com Page created on: 2026-11-10 12:19:08 UTC

The fight was intense and controversial, as Kreps outlanded Ali in punches, with a final tally of 115 to 78. Despite this, two judges awarded the fight to Ali, leading to mixed reactions, including criticism from veteran promoter Lou Di Bella. Ali, who fled Somalia's civil war and settled in London, expressed deep emotion after the win, dedicating it to her late father. She emphasized the importance of her victory for Somalia and hopes to inspire young people. Ali's journey, which includes being the first Somali boxer at the Olympics and a UNICEF ambassador, has been documented in the film "In the Shadows." somalia.content: U.S. maintains level 4 travel advisories for Uganda, DRC, Somalia and South Sudan - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY U.S. maintains level 4 travel advisories for Uganda, DRC, Somalia and South Sudan Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ by Timothy Cerullo Tuesday November 10, 2026 A collage of U.S. President Donald Trump and his Ugandan counterpart, Yoweri Museveni, during past separate events. Photo Trump/Museveni The United States government has issued its highest travel warning for four East African countries, including Uganda, urging its citizens and other foreigners to avoid visiting them because of security and health concerns. In a travel advisory issued on Monday, November 9, the U.S. Department of State placed Uganda, Somalia, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) under Level 4, the highest category in its four-level travel warning system. The four countries were flagged over terrorism, violent crime, kidnapping, political unrest and health risks, with the U.S. warning that its ability to provide emergency assistance to Americans in affected areas was limited. advertisements Uganda was specifically flagged over terrorism, armed robberies, home invasions, sexual assaults and the ongoing Ebola outbreak, which the U.S. government said had made it difficult to provide emergency assistance. The advisory also warned of possible terrorist attacks targeting religious institutions, schools, government buildings, police stations, transport centres and tourist attractions, particularly in major cities such as Kampala. On political stability, the U.S. warned that demonstrations could erupt without warning, especially during political events, adding that security officers had previously used tear gas, batons and rubber bullets against protesters. The U.S. government further raised concerns about Uganda's Anti-Homosexuality Act of 2023, which criminalises consensual same-sex relations and applies to both citizens and foreigners, with offenders facing life imprisonment. Somalia was also placed under Level 4 due to the risks of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, health concerns and landmines, with the U.S. government advising foreigners against travelling there for any reason. Other concerns raised by the U.S. included the systematic mistreatment of women and gay people, piracy, abuse of residents in rehabilitation centres and confiscation of passports by family members. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was also listed at Level 4 because of health concerns, crime, unrest, terrorism, and kidnapping, making it one of the countries foreigners have been advised to avoid. For Americans already in these countries, the U. S. government advised them to register with its Smart Traveller Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security updates and make it easier for diplomatic officials to contact them during emergencies. President Donald Trump's administration also urged its citizens in the affected countries to avoid demonstrations, remain alert in public places, exercise caution when walking or driving at night and prepare emergency departure plans. Uganda, Somalia, South Sudan and the DRC join 22 other countries on the U.S. travel advisory system's Level 4 list, including Afghanistan, Belarus, Burkina Faso, Myanmar, the Central African Republic, Chad, Haiti, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Libya, Mali, Niger, North Korea, Russia, Sudan, Syria, Ukraine and Yemen. "We issue Travel Advisories with Levels 1 to 4. Level 4 means do not travel. We assign Level 4 based on local conditions and our limited ability to help Americans there. These places are dangerous. Do not go for any reason," the U.S. government stated. somalia.title: Türkiye’s Ambassador Visits Maarif Schools as Oxford AQA Accreditation Opens Global Paths for Somali Students - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Türkiye's Ambassador Visits Maarif Schools as Oxford AQA Accreditation Opens Global Paths for Somali Students - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Education Benadir Türkiye’s Ambassador Visits Maarif Schools as Oxford AQA Accreditation Opens Global Paths for Somali Students November 10, 2026 5 min read MOGADISHU , Türkiye’s Ambassador to Somalia, Ferhat Alkan, visited the Somali International Maarif Schools in Mogadishu this week, meeting students and teachers at an institution that has operated in the country for a decade and become the first in Somalia to offer internationally accredited Oxford AQA examinations. The schools, operated by the Türkiye Maarif Foundation, have three campuses across Somalia and have graduated thousands of students over the past ten years. According to the embassy’s statement, the schools hold Oxford AQA-approved centre status, offering students education that meets international standards and creating pathways to higher education abroad that were previously unavailable inside the country. During his visit, Ambassador Alkan thanked the Maarif Foundation’s representative in Somalia, Dr. Selçuk Baş, along with teachers, students, and staff for their warm welcome and their ongoing efforts in advancing education. He said he was pleased to meet the children and young people, to hear their aspirations and hopes for the future, and stressed that investing in education is an investment in building a bright future for Somalia. A Decade of Growth and a First for Somalia The Maarif Foundation began its educational activities in Somalia in November 2016, taking over schools previously linked to the Gülen movement after the Somali government revoked their licenses at Türkiye’s request. The transition marked Somalia as one of the first African countries to transfer Gülen-affiliated institutions to Maarif, Türkiye’s official body for managing international education. The schools’ accreditation by Oxford AQA, a joint initiative between Oxford University Press and the UK’s AQA exam board, was a significant milestone. Before the accreditation, Somali students had to travel to neighbouring countries such as Kenya or Ethiopia to sit for IGCSE and A-Level examinations. Now they can take those exams inside Somalia, opening access to universities and employers in the UK, Europe, North America, and Asia without leaving home. The curriculum includes instruction in Somali, English, Turkish, and Arabic, and focuses on science, mathematics, and critical thinking. Officials say the goal is to equip Somali youth with the tools needed to compete on the global stage, while also preserving their cultural and linguistic heritage. The impact on individual students has been tangible. One former student, Abdishakur Abullarhi, told Hiiraan Online that “Maarif gave me the foundation I needed to study abroad,” adding that he has since returned to Somalia to contribute to the country’s reconstruction. Another student, born in Norway, said the school helped him learn Arabic and English and integrate culturally after returning to Somalia. The Bigger Picture: Türkiye’s Educational Footprint The Maarif schools are part of a broader educational partnership between Somalia and Türkiye that has deepened significantly over the past decade. Thousands of Somali students have studied in Turkish universities under the Türkiye Scholarships programme, with many graduates returning to work in government, education, healthcare, and engineering. In July 2026, over 300 Somali students graduated from Turkish universities in a ceremony in Ankara, as FTL Somalia reported on the graduation . The educational relationship extends to high-level institutional cooperation. In October 2026, Somalia’s Education Minister met with Türkiye’s Deputy Minister of Education in Ankara to discuss expanding cooperation, including vocational training and academic exchange programmes, as FTL Somalia reported on the ministerial meeting . Türkiye’s engagement in Somali education is not limited to Maarif. The Diyanet Foundation, Türkiye’s religious affairs authority, has also expanded cooperation with Somalia’s Ministry of Endowments and Islamic Affairs on religious education, Waqf management, and scholarships for Somali scholars, as FTL Somalia reported on the religious education partnership . Critical Note Ambassador Alkan’s visit is a routine diplomatic engagement, but it highlights a partnership that has produced concrete results. The Maarif schools are not just a Turkish project in Somalia. They are an educational institution that has become part of the country’s landscape, offering Somali families an option they did not have before: internationally accredited education without leaving home. The accreditation by Oxford AQA is the most significant achievement. It means that a student in Mogadishu can sit for the same exams as a student in London, and compete for the same university places. That is a meaningful change for a country where access to higher education has historically depended on family resources and the ability to travel abroad. But the Maarif model also raises questions that the visit did not address. The schools are operated by a Turkish state foundation, with a curriculum that includes Turkish language and culture. That is not a criticism, it is a reflection of the reality that education is never culturally neutral. The question is whether the Maarif schools are building Somali institutional capacity that will outlast Türkiye’s presence, or whether they are creating a dependency on external providers. The ambassador’s visit was a celebration of what has been built. The next decade will determine whether it is sustainable. somalia.summary: Türkiye’s Ambassador to Somalia, Ferhat Alkan, visited the Somali International Maarif Schools in Mogadishu, which recently became the first in Somalia to offer internationally accredited Oxford AQA examinations. Established by the Türkiye Maarif Foundation, these schools have been operational for a decade and have graduated thousands of students. The accreditation allows Somali students to take IGCSE and A-Level exams locally, previously requiring travel to neighboring countries, thus opening pathways to higher education globally. During his visit, Ambassador Alkan praised the efforts of the Maarif Foundation and emphasized the importance of investing in education for Somalia's future. The Maarif schools represent a significant educational partnership between Türkiye and Somalia, offering a curriculum that includes Somali, English, Turkish, and Arabic. While the schools provide valuable educational opportunities, questions remain about their long-term impact on Somali institutional capacity and dependency on external educational providers. The next decade will be crucial in determining the sustainability of this initiative.

somalia.title: Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke and the Making of Somalia’s First Republic - www.geeska.com
somalia.content: Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke and the making of Somalia’s first republic | Geeska Skip to main content Tuesday 10 November 2026 EN AR SO EN AR SO Home Current Analysis Opinion Culture Files Newsletter Multimedia Interviews Opinion Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke and the making of Somalia’s first republic 10 November, 2026 Image Mohamed Isse Trunji From pressing for early independence to unifying the institutions of a new republic, Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke helped shape Somalia’s founding years. Historian Mohamed Isse Trunji revisits his political rise, his vision of Somali unity and the unanswered questions surrounding his assassination 57 years ago. The history of the leaders who led the liberation movements in Somalia is largely ignored and disregarded among political scientists, historians and across the academic literature on Africa. Most of the leaders of these movements went to their graves without having an opportunity to tell their own stories. Somalia’s history includes many iconic figures like Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke, who shaped independence movements, governance, and social change across the country. It is not easy to tell the story about one of the founding fathers of the Constitution, twice Prime Minister, and lately President of the Republic. Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke was certainly one of the country’s most skillful and powerful politicians in the era after independence. He was born at Harardere in 1919. After having attended Quranic School, he completed his elementary education in 1936. From 1937 to 1943 he served as civil servant in the then Italian administration. At the same time, he brought his educational standard up to intermediate level. He entered the British Administration Civil Service in 1944. He joined the Somali Youth League (SYL) immediately after its foundation in 1943. He completed his secondary education in 1950-53 while still a Civil Servant, and got a scholarship to the “La Sapienza Universita’” of Rome where he graduated in political science in 1958. One year after his return from Italy, he was elected to the then Legislative Assembly for the electoral district of Gardo (Migiurtinia) as an SYL member in 1959. He was re-elected to Parliament in the first general elections after independence held 1964. The parliamentary records show the remarkable role he played in the parliamentary debates which distinguished him from most of the MPs. Demand for early independence As a senior SYL member, Abdirashid played a leading part in all significant political initiatives debated in the Legislative Assembly, first among them the demand for early independence. In fact, He sponsored a motion in the Legislative Assembly calling for early independence “possibilmente entro il 31 Dicembre dell’anno in corso”, (possibly before the end of the year), on August 17. (Il Corriere della Somalia. 19.8.1959). One of the motives for presenting the motion, he explained, was the perceived Ethiopian threat of territorial annexation designed to block the planned union between Somalia and the British Protectorate of Somaliland. A second reason cited in the motion was the realization that “grazie alla leale e effettiva osservanza da parte dell’ autorita’ amministrative degli obblighi assunti, il Paese aveva gia’ conseguito l’idoneita’ a governarsi” (thanks to the loyal and effective observance of the Administering Power of its obligations, the country had already acquired the ability to govern itself. (Il Corriere della Somalia 20.8.1959; G. Costanzo, p, 62) The history of the leaders who led the liberation movements in Somalia is largely ignored and disregarded among political scientists, historians and across the academic literature on Africa. Most of the leaders of these movements went to their graves without having an opportunity to tell their own stories. As a matter of fact, the Ethiopian government was deeply disturbed by the proposed unification of the Protectorate with the Trust Territory, and remonstrated with Britain and United States regarding a widely publicized statement by Mr. Lennox Boyd (British Colonial Secretary at the time) about constitutional progress in Somaliland and a possible merger with Somalia. The motion was overwhelmingly approved by the Legislative Assembly on August 25, 1959 (Il Corriere della Somalia August 26, 1959) The motion took effect immediately and Somalia became independent on July 1, 1960, i.e., six months ahead of the original date of December 2, 1960, stipulated by the Trusteeship Agreement between Italy and the United Nations. (General Assembly Resolution 289 (IV) of November 21, 1949) Abdirashid Prime Minister On 26 June 1960, British Protectorate of Somaliland became independent State. It united with the UN Trust Territory of Somalia to create the Somali Republic on 1 July 1960. Aden Abdulla Osman, in his capacity as provisional president called Abdirashid, a rising political figure, to form a united government. At the end of long consultations, Sharmarke formed a Cabinet of 15-members, in practice a clan coalition, dominated by the SYL party; in association with two other equally clan based northern parties: the Somali National League (SNL) and the United Somali Party (USP). Clan representation was within the bounds in support of the unwritten notion of clan balance. On August 13, 1960, the government presented its political programme to the National Assembly, gaining a large vote of confidence: 97 in favour and 3 against. Two important constitutional developments occurred in 1960-1961: (a) the approval of the Constitution in a popular refrendum and, (b) the election of Aden Abdulla as full time Head of State. The best qualified man for this task After winning a full time presidential term of office in 1961, Aden Abdulla had again designated Abdirashid as Prime Minister. The decision of the President came as a result of intensive informal consultations with political parties and influential individuals. As the consensus emerging from the consultations appeared to be in favour of the ongoing Prime Minister, Aden Abdulla again called Abdirashid to form a government. In a brief statement to the press, the President announced: “I designated Abdirashid to form a new government and he accepted the designation with “reserve”, adding “I am sure, as I was in July last year, that the designated Prime Minister is the best qualified man for this task”.(Somali News July 14, 1961). When the two regions were joined in July 1960, they had two different judicial systems, different currencies, different organizations and conditions of service for the army, police force and civil servants. His government had achieved enormous progress in the field of integration. On 19 August Abdirashid presented the list of his cabinet to the National Assembly and obtained the vote of confidence with a majority of 94 to 19. (Government Activities, from Independence until today, 11 July, 1960 - 31 December 1963. Presidency of Council of Ministers, Mogadiscio 1964, p, 19) . Abdirashid was one of few Somali MPs with University degree and long experience in administration. One of Abdirashid’s qualities was his ability to compromise, which had served him well in dealing with an often fractious Parliament. Abdirashid was also known for his close ties with influential religious sects based in the capital, which further enhanced his status as political campaigner. Integration problem During his four-year tenure as Prime Minister (1960-1964) he gained popularity for his policy of integration between the two regions of former British Protectorate of Somaliland and former UN trust territory of Somalia. When the two regions were joined in July 1960, they had two different judicial systems, different currencies, different organizations and conditions of service for the army, police force and civil servants. His government had achieved enormous progress in the field of integration. In fact, with the help of the United Nations Consultative Commission for Integration, the institutions of the two territories were quickly unified. Priority was given to unifying the Judiciary and civil service. A single legal system was approved. The fiscal and accounting systems were unified; the police and the national army were integrated. Greater Somalia Policy The Greater Somalia Policy refers to a long-standing intractable pan-Somali nationalism ideology aimed at unifying all ethnic Somali inhabited territories in the Horn of Africa into a single independent State. The intractability of this question was eloquently expressed by Premier Abdirashid: “Our misfortune”, he said, “is that our neighboring countries, with whom, like the rest of Africa, we seek to promote constructive and harmonious relations, are not our neighbors. Our neighbors are our kinsmen whose citizenship has been falsified by indiscriminate boundary “arrangements”. Thy have to move across artificial frontier to their pasture land. They occupy the same terrains and pursue the same pastoral economy as ourselves. We speak the same language. We share the sane creed, the same culture, and the same traditions. How can we regard our brothers as foreigners? Of course we all have a strong and very natural desire to unite. The first step in this direction was taken in 1960 when the Somaliland Protectorate was united to Somalia. This act was not an act of “colonialism”, or “expansionism” or “annexation”. (“The Somali Peninsula. A New Light on Imperial Motives”. Information Service of the Somali Government, 1962,). The assassination of the President is surrounded by a “jumble of speculation”, the narration of which is outside the purview of this piece. However, suffice it here to say that, though the assassination took place 57 years ago, key questions about Abdirashid’s death remain unanswered. External factor working against the Greater Somalia scheme emerged in 1963 with the establishment of the Organization of African Union (OAU), now African Union (AU), whose Charter recognizes the inviolability of the excising African borders inherited by the European colonial powers. Abdirashid President of the Republic The National Assembly on June 10, 1967, elected Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke to lead the country over the coming six years as Head of State. Abdirashid got 73 against 50 votes in favour of Aden Abdulla Osman, the former President. Aden Abdulla did not only concede defeat but, even though his term of office was not due to expire until July 6, 1967, he wrote to the President of the National Assembly asking Parliament to accept earlier transfer of power from June 30 at 6:00pm. He suggested this in order to allow the newly-elected President to preside over the celebrations marking Independence Day on 1 July. The National Assembly approved the resignation of President Aden Abdulla, seven days ahead of the official expiry of his term of office. The killing of the President On 15 October 1969, Radio Mogadiscio gave the shocking news that the President of the Republic had been shot dead at about 12:45pm in Las Anod by a rogue policeman, less than three full years into his presidential term. The President was visiting the northern provinces of the country, hit by famine and drought. The assassination of the President is surrounded by a “jumble of speculation”, the narration of which is outside the purview of this piece. However, suffice it here to say that, though the assassination took place 57 years ago, key questions about Abdirashid’s death remain unanswered. somalia.summary: Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke played a pivotal role in the establishment of Somalia’s first republic, advocating for early independence and unifying the nation’s institutions. Born in 1919, Sharmarke's political journey began with the Somali Youth League, leading to his election to the Legislative Assembly in 1959. He was instrumental in pushing for Somalia's independence, which was achieved on July 1, 1960, ahead of schedule. As Prime Minister from 1960 to 1964, he focused on integrating the former British Protectorate of Somaliland and the UN Trust Territory of Somalia, successfully unifying their judicial and civil systems. Sharmarke later became President in 1967 but was assassinated in 1969, raising numerous unanswered questions about his death. His legacy remains significant, as he is remembered for his vision of Somali unity and the challenges he faced, particularly regarding the Greater Somalia Policy, which sought to unify all Somali-inhabited territories in the Horn of Africa.

somalia.title: Unlocking Somalia's Investment Potential- Opportunities in the Blue Economy, Fisheries, Energy and Agriculture - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Unlocking Somalia's Investment Potential- Opportunities in the Blue Economy, Fisheries, Energy and Agriculture - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME OPINION Unlocking Somalia's Investment Potential- Opportunities in the Blue Economy, Fisheries, Energy and Agriculture Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Guleid Osman Tuesday November 10, 2026 Debt relief, regional integration and a new investment law have repositioned Somalia as an early-mover market. This article examines the domestic and foreign investment opportunities across four connected sectors the blue economy, fisheries, energy, and agriculture and the conditions under which they can be realized. Introduction For much of the past three decades, Somalia has been discussed in terms of fragility rather than opportunity. That framing is becoming outdated. Since reaching the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Completion Point in December 2023, the country has eliminated almost all of its legacy external debt, joined the East African Community, and enacted the Somalia Investment Law 2025. Foreign direct investment has risen steadily, reaching US$834 million in 2025, while the Somali diaspora transfers more than US$3 billion a year in personal remittances alone. The opportunities are substantial and interlinked. Somalia possesses the longest coastline on mainland Africa, fish stocks that are harvested at a fraction of their sustainable yield, some of the continent's strongest solar and wind resources, and a livestock export trade that crossed the billion-dollar mark in 2025. At the same time, electricity remains among the most expensive in the world, cold-chain infrastructure is almost absent, and only a small share of irrigable land is cultivated. This article argues that the greatest value lies at the intersection of these sectors. Affordable renewable power makes cold storage viable; cold storage makes fish and meat exportable; and modernized ports convert exportable products into foreign-exchange earnings. Investors—domestic, diaspora and foreign—who approach Somalia's economy as a connected system rather than as isolated sectors are best placed to capture that value. The Investment Climate Somalia's macroeconomic position has changed fundamentally in the past three years. In December 2023 the Executive Boards of the IMF and the World Bank's International Development Association approved the country's HIPC Completion Point, reducing external public debt from US$5.3 billion at end-2018 to approximately US$0.6 billion and unlocking about US$4.5 billion in debt service relief (IMF). Weeks earlier, Somalia had been admitted to the East African Community, giving Somali producers preferential access to a regional market of roughly 300 million people (The EastAfrican). The economy is growing, though more slowly than before. Real GDP expanded by 4.1 percent in 2024; the IMF projects 3.0 percent for 2025 and 3.3 percent for 2026, citing reduced foreign aid and adverse weather as the principal constraints (Ecofin Agency). Nominal GDP is estimated at about US$14.2 billion in 2026 (IMF World Economic Outlook, via Fermor). Fiscal policy remains anchored by an IMF Extended Credit Facility, under which disbursements have reached US$100 million, and the Fund has noted progress in Central Bank supervision and preparations to reintroduce the Somali shilling (Channel Africa). Investor interest has followed. According to UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2026, FDI inflows rose from US$601 million in 2021 to US$834 million in 2025, while the stock of foreign investment grew from US$4.3 billion to US$7.2 billion over the same period (Dawan Africa). Relative to the size of the economy, these inflows are significant: World Bank data put FDI at 6.4 percent of GDP in 2024 (World Bank WDI). The legal framework has matured in parallel. The Somalia Investment Law 2025 provides a clearer and more predictable basis for foreign participation, and the Somalia Investment Promotion Agency (SOMINVEST) serves as the principal point of entry. Somalia has been a member of the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency since March 2020, making political-risk insurance available to foreign investors (World Bank), and a public–private partnership law has been in preparation since debt relief was secured. The Blue Economy: Ports, Logistics and Offshore Resources Somalia's 3,333-kilometre coastline and approximately one million square kilometers of maritime territory lie alongside the shipping lanes linking the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean (US Commercial Service). Geography alone makes the country a natural candidate for maritime trade, transshipment and logistics. The investable opportunities fall broadly into three categories: port infrastructure and associated free zones, services linked to offshore energy exploration, and a range of smaller coastal enterprises. Ports and Free Zones Port development has already attracted the largest single foreign investments in the country. At Berbera, DP World operates a 30-year concession that began in 2017 and carries a planned investment of up to US$442 million across two phases, including a new quay, an expanded container yard and the Berbera Economic Zone (Gulf News). At Bosaso, a 30-year concession agreed with Puntland envisages a US$336 million multipurpose upgrade, also in two phases (Trade Arabia). The Port of Mogadishu, managed by Turkey's Albayrak Group, is one of the Federal Government's largest sources of domestic revenue, and in July 2026 the President discussed plans for an entirely new port to meet the capital's growing needs (Dawan Africa). Smaller ports, including Kismayo, Hobyo and Garacad which received its first vessel in 2022—have also attracted interest from public and private investors (Maritime Executive). Across all these facilities the constraints are similar: insufficient berths, warehousing, cold storage, cargo-handling equipment and professional management. Each of these gaps represents a contract-sized opportunity accessible to domestic logistics firms that need not finance an entire concession. Offshore Oil and Gas Somalia's offshore hydrocarbon potential has long attracted speculation; it is now being tested. Under a 2024 intergovernmental framework, the Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO) acquired 3D seismic data across Blocks 142, 152 and 153 and began drilling the Curad-1 exploration well in Block 153 in April 2026 (Oil Price). The reported fiscal terms are favorable to the operator, with royalties capped at 5 percent and cost recovery of up to 90 percent of production—an explicit trade-off of early revenue for reduced exploration risk. Resource estimates of 30 billion barrels or more remain un-risked and unproven (bne Intelli News). For most investors, the realistic near-term opportunity lies not in upstream equity but in supporting services: supply bases, logistics, fuel storage and local-content provision. Coastal Enterprise Beyond ports and hydrocarbons, the blue economy offers a range of smaller opportunities well suited to domestic and diaspora capital. These include ship chandlery, bunkering and repair services, particularly at Bosaso and Berbera; coastal tourism and hospitality, which the Ministry of Foreign Affairs identifies as a largely overlooked sector (Ministry of Foreign Affairs); and salt production, seaweed cultivation and desalination. Fisheries: Closing the Gap Between Catch and Potential Few sectors illustrate the distance between Somalia's resources and its realized output as clearly as fisheries. According to data submitted to the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission, the national catch reached 76,026 tons in 2024, a 30 percent increase on the previous year, of which yellowfin tuna accounted for 18,635 tons (Dawan Africa). Estimates of sustainable yield vary considerably but are uniformly higher: the US Commercial Service cites a potential well above 200,000 tons a year (US Commercial Service), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs refers to some 300,000 tons of fish and 10,000 tons of crustaceans (Ministry of Foreign Affairs), and a 2025 analysis by the Somali Development and Reconstruction Bank places the figure between 380,000 and 500,000 tons. Meanwhile, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing is estimated to cost the country around US$300 million annually (Daily Maverick). The constraint, in short, is not the resource but the vessels, ice, storage, processing capacity and market access needed to capture it onshore. An Improving Policy Environment Several recent policy developments have strengthened the case for investment. In March 2026 the Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy published revised exclusive economic zone license fees for foreign-flagged vessels and for Somali-flagged vessels not wholly owned by Somali citizens; crucially, companies that invest in onshore economic activity within the same fishing year may qualify for discounted fees (Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy). This rewards landing and processing in Somalia rather than at sea. Foreign vessels remain excluded from the first 24 nautical miles, preserving space for domestic small-scale fleets. In October 2026 the Cabinet approved a nine-member board for the National Fishing Company, providing a formal state counterpart for joint ventures. The World Bank's US$50 million Badmaal project is concurrently financing landing-site infrastructure, community capacity and a national Fisheries Information Management System. Investment Priorities The most immediate opportunity is the cold chain. A value-chain study prepared for the World Bank found that, without integrated chilling, catches are routinely exposed to sea temperatures of 25–30°C, causing rapid spoilage, lost value and, in tuna, histamine-related food-safety risks (Matis). Ice plants, solar-powered cold rooms and insulated transport therefore offer a comparatively low-risk entry with immediate returns. Processing and export certification form the logical next step. Tuna canning, frozen lobster and dried products can serve Gulf and East African markets in the near term, while access to European markets will require an accredited competent authority and sanitary controls—an investment that early entrants should anticipate. Domestic semi-industrial fleets of 15–24-metre longliners and multipurpose vessels, financed by diaspora equity, represent a further opportunity, as do jetties, fish markets and auction halls at ports such as Mogadishu, Kismayo, Hobyo, Eyl and Bosaso, often co-financed through Badmaal. Finally, the Juba and Shabelle rivers and more than 10,000 square kilometers of inland water offer scope for aquaculture, while coastal sites suit seaweed and sea-cucumber farming (SATG). Energy: From Diesel Dependence to Renewable Opportunity Somalia's electricity sector presents a striking paradox. Consumers paid an average of approximately US$0.61 per kilowatt-hour in 2023—and more than US$1 in some areas served by private diesel generators—while more than 80 percent of generation still relies on imported diesel (Ecofin Agency, citing the World Bank). Yet the country receives average solar irradiance above 6 kWh per square meter per day and annual mean wind speeds exceeding 8 meters per second across most regions (Ministry of Energy and Water Resources), endowments that rank among the strongest in Africa. Installed solar capacity stood at only about 51 MW at the end of 2023 (PV magazine), and roughly half the population has access to electricity, falling to around 31 percent in rural areas. The government has set a target of 50 percent renewable electricity by 2028. The gap between today's diesel-based costs and the cost of new solar-plus storage capacity constitutes the core of the investment case. Market Structure and Regulation Somalia has no national grid. Electricity is supplied by private electricity service providers (ESPs) operating city-level networks and mini-grids, the largest being BECO in Mogadishu. This structure is unusual: the counterparties for new generation are private companies, and the sector already operates on private capital. The Electricity Act of 2023 established the National Electricity Authority (NEA) as the federal regulator, separating regulation from the policy role of the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources. NEA is now putting in place the regulatory architecture that investors require. This includes interim licensing instruments for generation and distribution developed with World Bank support; cost-of-service tariff regulation designed to align ESP tariffs with efficient costs and to reflect donor-financed assets; a national framework for independent power producers (IPPs) and standardized power purchase agreements (PPAs), supported under the EU-funded SDIT/GEED program; and draft Somali National Electrical Installation Guidelines, currently under stakeholder consultation. Program and Pipeline Development finance is building a substantial pipeline. The World Bank's US$100 million ASCENT Somalia project, running to 2028, seeks to expand access to clean energy through private-sector participation. Its flagship is a 45 MW solar photovoltaic plant with 140 MWh of battery storage at the Jazeera power station in Mogadishu, to be connected to BECO's network (Taiyang News). The Somali Electricity Sector Recovery Project is financing sector institutions, hybrid plants and the solarization of public facilities, including 585 public institutions (education and health facilities). The African Development Bank approved US$23 million in 2023 for solar generation and network upgrades in Bosaso, and the World Bank is preparing support for a first 500 kV transmission line that would begin to link Somalia's fragmented regional systems (ITSF). Opportunities for Investors For international and regional IPPs, the principal opportunity lies in grid-scale solar-plus-storage and wind plants selling power to ESPs under PPAs, once the national IPP/PPA framework and licenses are in force; coastal wind near Hobyo, Bosaso and Kismayo remain largely untapped. Domestic ESPs and investors can hybridize existing diesel networks, consolidate and upgrade city utilities, and extend distribution under regulated tariffs. Distributed energy town mini-grids, commercial and industrial rooftop solar, and productive-use systems such as solar irrigation pumps and cold rooms links the energy sector directly to agriculture and fisheries. Clean cooking and liquefied petroleum gas offer a further market, given the continued dominance of charcoal in household energy use. Agriculture and Livestock: Building on a Billion-Dollar Export Base Agriculture in its broadest sense crops, livestock and fisheries accounts for approximately 72 percent of Somalia's GDP (Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation). The sector combines one of the country's great commercial successes, the livestock trade, with one of its largest untapped assets: irrigable land along the Juba and Shabelle rivers. Livestock Somalia's national herd is estimated at 56 to 57 million animals, supporting exports of between four and six million head a year, predominantly sheep and goats destined for Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Qatar (Dawan Africa). Central Bank data show export earnings rising from US$311 million in 2018 to approximately US$970 million in 2024, with 2025 projected to exceed US$1 billion for the first time (Food Business MEA). Market conditions have moved in Somalia's favor, conflict in Sudan and Australia's planned phase-out of live sheep exports by sea by 2028 have reduced competition in Gulf markets. The strategic opportunity is to move from exporting live animals to exporting value-added products. Export-certified abattoirs and chilled-meat facilities, feedlots and commercial fodder production, veterinary and quarantine services, hides and skins processing, and camel milk and dairy enterprises would each capture margins currently earned outside the country. Crops and Irrigation Of roughly 700,000 hectares suitable for pump or flood-recession irrigation, only about 110,800 hectares are currently irrigated less than half the area irrigated before the civil war (SOMINVEST). Somalia is nonetheless a significant global producer of sesame, grown principally in Lower Juba and Middle Shabelle. Under the FAO Hand-in-Hand Initiative, the government has presented an US$82.1 million investment case to raise sesame output by 50 percent, from 50,000 tons, alongside cases for maize, dairy and fodder (FAO). The European Union and Sweden are financing the rehabilitation of some 350 kilometers of irrigation canals on the two rivers (European Commission). These developments open several avenues for investors. Sesame hulling, oil extraction and tahini production would add value to a crop currently exported largely unprocessed, for which demand from China and the East African Community is strong. Commercial banana, lime and horticulture farms potentially organized throughout-grower schemes—could revive what was once a significant export trade. Irrigation services and solar-powered pumping address the gap between irrigated and irrigable land, while post-harvest storage, cold chains and phytosanitary laboratories are prerequisites for meeting export standards. Frankincense and myrrh from the north-east offer a high-value niche, and agricultural finance and insurance remain underdeveloped for smallholders who typically farm between 0.2 and 3 hectares. Domestic and Foreign Investors: Complementary Roles Somalia's largest pool of investable capital is domestic in origin. Central Bank data show total inward transfers reaching a record US$6.78 billion in 2025, of which individual remittances accounted for US$3.13 billion, or roughly 24 percent of GDP (The EastAfrican, citing the Central Bank of Somalia). Redirecting even a modest share of these flows from consumption into long-term productive equity would rival annual foreign direct investment. Different categories of investors bring distinct strengths. Domestic firms and business groups contribute local knowledge, established networks and existing operations in electricity supply, trade and telecommunications, and are well placed to lead mini-grid expansion, cold-chain development, fish markets and agro-processing. Diaspora investors combine hard-currency capital with international skills and a higher tolerance for local risk; commercial farms, fishing vessels, processing plants, hospitality and commercial solar suit their profile, and the National Diaspora Policy ratified in 2023 provides a framework for deeper engagement. Gulf and Turkish strategic investors, with established trade ties and existing port and logistics operations, are natural partners for ports, free zones, meat processing, large-scale agriculture and upstream energy, supported by bilateral investment treaties with Turkey, Germany and Egypt. International IPPs and specialist operators bring technology and project-finance experience for grid-scale renewables, tuna processing and certified abattoirs. Development finance institutions including the IDA Private Sector Window, the African Development Bank, IFC and EU blending facilities provide the concessional and risk-sharing capital that first-of-kind projects require. The Baidoa hybrid solar project demonstrates how these roles can be combined. In January 2023 MIGA issued its first guarantee in Somalia US$5.67 million for up to 15 years covering Kube Energy's investment in a plant that supplies the United Nations mission under a power purchase agreement (MIGA). A creditworthy offtake, political-risk cover and a first-loss layer from the IDA Private Sector Window together made the project bankable. The
somalia.summary: Somalia is emerging as a promising investment destination, particularly in the blue economy, fisheries, energy, and agriculture sectors. Following significant debt relief and the enactment of the Somalia Investment Law 2025, foreign direct investment (FDI) has surged, reaching $834 million in 2025. The country boasts the longest coastline in mainland Africa, abundant fish stocks, and strong renewable energy resources, yet faces challenges such as high electricity costs and underdeveloped infrastructure. The article highlights the interconnectedness of these sectors, emphasizing that investments in renewable energy can enhance cold storage capabilities, thereby boosting fish and meat exports. Additionally, Somalia's fisheries sector shows vast potential, with sustainable yields estimated at over 200,000 tons annually, yet current catches remain significantly lower due to inadequate infrastructure. The government is actively improving the investment climate, making it an opportune time for both domestic and foreign investors to engage in Somalia's evolving economy.

somalia.title: Somalia, U.S. discuss security transition and fight against al-Shabab, ISIS - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia, U.S. discuss security transition and fight against al-Shabab, ISIS - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME SECURITY Somalia, U.S. discuss security transition and fight against al-Shabab, ISIS Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Monday November 9, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi met with U.S. Embassy Chargé d’Affaires Ruth Anne Stevens-Klitz in Mogadishu on Sunday to discuss military cooperation, counterterrorism operations and the transfer of security responsibilities from African Union forces to the Somali National Army. The meeting focused on ongoing operations against al-Shabab and ISIS, the future of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) and Somalia's security transition plan. advertisements Both sides discussed the importance of ensuring that Somali security forces have the necessary training, equipment and operational capacity before assuming responsibilities currently held by African Union troops. Fiqi briefed the U.S. diplomat on military operations against al-Shabab and reaffirmed the federal government's commitment to building a capable national army that can maintain security and protect Somalia's sovereignty. The discussions also addressed the recent handover of a former AUSSOM military base in Barawe, Lower Shabelle region, to the Somali National Army. The transfer is part of ongoing efforts to gradually shift security responsibilities from African Union forces to Somali troops as the country works toward greater control of its national security operations. Fiqi emphasized the importance of continued U.S. assistance, particularly in military training, capacity-building and operational support for Somali forces. The meeting comes as Somalia prepares to assume greater responsibility for its security amid continuing military operations against al-Shabab and concerns over the pace of the African Union troop withdrawal. The United States remains a key security partner for Somalia, providing training and operational assistance to Somali forces involved in counterterrorism operations. The federal government has repeatedly emphasized that a successful security transition will depend on strengthening the capabilities of Somali troops while maintaining coordination with international partners. No new military assistance package or formal agreement was announced following the meeting. somalia.content: Türkiye, Somalia discuss security ties as peacekeeping troops begin withdrawal - TRT World LIVE TV POLITICS TÜRKİYE WAR ON GAZA BIZTECH INFOGRAPHICS FEATURES OPINION WAR ON IRAN TÜRKİYE 1 min read Türkiye, Somalia discuss security ties as peacekeeping troops begin withdrawal Talks in Mogadishu focus on counterterrorism, the fight against Al Shabab terror group and continued military cooperation as Somalia faces a changing security landscape. Share Ferhat Alkan met Somalia’s National Security Adviser Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed in Mogadishu on November 9 2026. (Turkish Embassy in Somalia) Türkiye and Somalia have discussed military and security developments, counterterrorism efforts and bilateral cooperation as troop-contributing countries begin withdrawing forces from the African Union peacekeeping mission in Somalia. The discussions took place during a meeting between Turkish Ambassador to Somalia Ferhat Alkan and Somalia’s National Security Adviser Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed in Mogadishu. “Türkiye continues to contribute to the peace, stability, and security of Somalia, as it has in the past,” the Turkish Embassy said in a statement on Tuesday. Somalia’s Office of the National Security Adviser said the talks also covered political developments, the fight against Al Shabab and broader bilateral cooperation. The Somali official expressed appreciation for Türkiye’s longstanding friendship and support, while stressing the importance of continued coordination to maintain stability, according to the statement. السنغال في تصفيات أمم إفريقيا 2027 إسلام عيد الإثنين 09/نوفمبر/2026 - 11:12 م منتخب السودان أعلن الغاني كواسي أبياه المدير الفني لمنتخب السودان، قائمة صقور الجديان استعدادًا لمواجهتي السنغال، ضمن منافسات الجولة الثالثة والرابعة من التصفيات المؤهلة إلى بطولة كأس الأمم الإفريقية 2027. وشهدت تلك القائمة استبعاد محمد عبد الرحمن قائد نادي الهلال السوداني، إلى جانب محمد أسد لاعب المريخ، وياسين حامد الهلال السوداني والمرشح لجائزة أفضل لاعب داخل القارة الإفريقية، وشادي برجلان لاعب دين بوش الهولندي. قائمة المنتخب السوداني لمواجهتي السنغال وجاءت قائمة منتخب السودان لمواجهتي السنغال في التصفيات المؤهلة إلى نهائيات كأس أمم إفريقيا 2027، على النحو التالي.. حراسة المرمى: محمد المصطفى، محمد عبدالله كدياباً، مصطفى عيسى محمد. خط الدفاع: ياسر عوض، شادي عزالدين، أحمد عبدالمنعم طبنجة، مازن محمدين، مصطفى كرشوم، محمد كسرى، عبدالرحمن كوكو، مصعب مكين. خط الوسط: صلاح عادل، أبوعاقلة عبدالله، عمار طيفور، والي الدين بوغبا، عبدالرؤوف يعقوب، أحمد حامد التش، معتز هاشم التوزة، السماني الصاوي. خط الهجوم: أبوبكر عيسى، موسى كانتي، عامر عبدالله، الجزولي نوح، ياسر مزمل، محمد عيسى، أمجد قلق. قائمة منتخب السودان موعد مواجهتي السنغال والسودان ويخوض منتخب السودان مواجهته الأولى أمام السنغال يوم 12 نوفمبر الجاري، على ملعب ليوبولد سيدار سنجور، في تمام الساعة التاسعة مساءً بتوقيت القاهرة والسودان. ويتجدد اللقاء بين المنتخبين يوم 16 من الشهر ذاته، على ملعب جوبا الوطني، في تمام الساعة الثالثة عصرًا بتوقيت القاهرة والسودان. ويحتل منتخب السودان المركز الثالث في المجموعة العاشرة برصيد 3 نقاط، جمعها من فوز وخسارة، ضمن مشواره في التصفيات المؤهلة إلى كأس الأمم الإفريقية 2027. facebook twitter whats شارك football.summary: أعلن كواسي أبياه، المدير الفني لمنتخب السودان، قائمة اللاعبين الذين سيشاركون في مواجهتي السنغال ضمن تصفيات كأس الأمم الإفريقية 2027. تم استبعاد بعض اللاعبين البارزين مثل محمد عبد الرحمن قائد نادي الهلال، ومحمد أسد من المريخ، وياسين حامد المحترف في قيرغيزستان. بينما شهدت القائمة عودة أبوعاقلة عبدالله ومازن محمدين، بالإضافة إلى عبدالرؤوف يعقوب، المرشح لجائزة أفضل لاعب في إفريقيا. تضم القائمة 26 لاعبًا، منهم حراس المرمى محمد المصطفى ومحمد عبدالله كدياباً، والمدافعون ياسر عوض وشادي عزالدين، ولاعبو الوسط صلاح عادل وأحمد حامد التش. ستقام المباراة الأولى في 12 نوفمبر على ملعب ليوبولد سيدار سنجور، بينما ستقام المباراة الثانية في 16 نوفمبر على ملعب جوبا الوطني. يحتل منتخب السودان المركز الثالث في مجموعته برصيد 3 نقاط.

football.content: 3 تغييرات مرتقبة على تشكيل السودان قبل موقعتي السنغال 3 تغييرات مرتقبة على تشكيل السودان قبل موقعتي السنغال مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول 3 تغييرات مرتقبة على تشكيل السودان قبل موقعتي السنغال منتخب السودان (Facebook/ SFA) 9 نوفمبر 2026 3 تغييرات مرتقبة على تشكيل السودان قبل موقعتي السنغال السودان السنغال تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' وصل عبد الرحمن كوكو ومحمد عيسى نجما منتخب السودان، إلى العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي يوم الإثنين 9 نوفمبر/ تشرين الثاني، وانضمّا إلى المعسكر استعدادًا للمواجهتين المرتقبتين أمام السنغال يومي 12 و16 من الشهر الحالي، ضمن الجولتين 3 و4 من تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية 2027 . ويعزز وصول الثنائي صفوف المنتخب السوداني بقيادة المدرب الغاني جيمس كواسي أبياه، الذي استقبل عددًا كبيرًا من المحترفين في الخارج، بالإضافة إلى عناصر الهلال والمريخ الموجودين بالعاصمة كيغالي وخاضوا مباريات تنافسية قوية بالدوري الرواندي. أبياه سيجري 3 تغييرات في تشكيل السودان تأهبًا للسنغال ستشهد تشكيلة "صقور الجديان" 3 تغييرات مقارنة باللقاءين السابقين أمام إثيوبيا وموزمبيق، في ظل غياب بعض العناصر وعودة أخرى يعول عليها المدرب في هاتين المباراتين الحاسمتين لمسيرة التأهل. ومن المتوقع أن يعود أبوعاقلة عبد الله لدعم مركز محور الارتكاز في منتخب السودان، بينما يُنتظر أن يسجل الجزولي نوح حضوره الأول بالتصفيات الحالية في مركز خط الهجوم، في حين فرض تألق السماني الصاوي وجاهزيته الفنية في المعسكر نفسه ضمن خيارات أبياه للمباراة بعد مشاركته في مباراة ودية خاضها المنتخب ضد رديف فريق الهلال. اقرأ أيضًا: مدرب السودان يحظى بدعم هائل قبل موقعتي السنغال أبياه يقف بين الثقة والإقالة قبل موقعة السنغال وشهدت قائمة المنتخب السوداني لمواجهتي "أسود التيرانغا" عدد دعوات قياسي وغير مسبوق من جانب المدرب كواسي أبياه، إذ ضمت أكثر من 35 لاعبًا بينهم 19 من فريقي الهلال والمريخ، إلى جانب 7 من نجوم منتخب الشباب. وكشفت مصادر موثوقة لموقع "winwin" أن المدرب الغاني، الذي يدخل عامه الرابع في قيادة المنتخب السوداني، سيقلص القائمة لاحقًا لتستقر على 25 لاعبًا فقط وذلك قبل السفر إلى داكار. ويسعى أبياه لقيادة السودان إلى تحقيق نتيجة إيجابية أمام السنغال لتعزيز حظوظه في التأهل للنهائيات الأفريقية للمرة الثانية تواليًا، خاصة أن تعثره قد يضعه في مواجهة خطر الإقالة، مما قد ينهي مسيرته مع الفريق ويحرمه من مواصلة نجاحاته بعد بلوغه 3 نهائيات قارية العام الماضي. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق رياضات التنس كرة football.summary: تستعد منتخب السودان لكرة القدم لإجراء ثلاثة تغييرات على تشكيلته قبل مواجهتيه المرتقبتين ضد السنغال في تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية 2027، المقررتين في 12 و16 نوفمبر. وصل اللاعبان عبد الرحمن كوكو ومحمد عيسى إلى كيغالي للانضمام إلى المعسكر، مما يعزز صفوف الفريق بقيادة المدرب الغاني جيمس كواسي أبياه. من المتوقع أن يعود أبوعاقلة عبد الله لدعم محور الارتكاز، بينما سيظهر الجزولي نوح لأول مرة في التصفيات الحالية في مركز الهجوم. كما أن تألق السماني الصاوي يجعله خيارًا قويًا للمشاركة بعد أدائه الجيد في مباراة ودية. قائمة المنتخب تضم أكثر من 35 لاعبًا، مع توقع تقليصها إلى 25 لاعبًا قبل السفر إلى داكار. يسعى أبياه لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية لتعزيز فرص التأهل، حيث أن أي تعثر قد يهدد مستقبله مع الفريق.

زينباور محاصَر.. تحديات قارية شاقة تنتظر الهلال السوداني الألماني جوزيف زينباور مدرب الهلال السودني (Facebook/ Al Hilal S.C) 9 نوفمبر 2026 زينباور محاصَر.. تحديات قارية شاقة تنتظر الهلال السوداني الهلال السوداني جوزيف زينباور دوري أبطال أفريقيا كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أثار تراجع المستوى الفني وتذبذب نتائج فريق الهلال السوداني في النسخة الحالية من الدوري الرواندي قلقًا جماهيريًا كبيرًا، لا سيما بعد تحقيقه انتصارات بشق الأنفس، عقب الهيمنة التي فرضها على الأندية وتتويجه باللقب في الموسم الماضي. وقد وضعت هذه النتائج مدرب الفريق جوزيف زينباور أمام تحديات مضاعفة، حيث انشغلت منصات التواصل الاجتماعي بمقارنة أداء الفريق الحالي تحت قيادة المدرب الألماني بما قدمه في الموسم المنصرم مع المدرب السابق لورينتيو ريجيكامب. وقد تسبب هذا التراجع في موجة من الغضب الجماهيري التي باتت تضغط على الإدارة، مما يجعل منصب المدرب مهددًا في حال استمر إخفاق النتائج في تلبية الطموحات. المغامرة القارية تحدد مصير زينباور في الهلال السوداني يجد المدرب زينباور نفسه أمام تحد كبير يتمثل في ضرورة بلوغ ربع نهائي دوري أبطال أفريقيا على الأقل، وهو الدور الذي توقف عنده الفريق في النسختين الماضيتين، خاصة في ظل الدعم الكبير الذي حظي به من إدارة النادي عبر استقطاب محترفين أجانب مميزين، وتوفير معسكرات تحضيرية مثالية للمنافسة بقوة في البطولة. واصطدم مدرب الهلال السوداني برحيل أبرز نجومه المحترف البوروندي جون كلود لنادي الأهلي طرابلس الليبي، فيما استعاد المالي أداما كوليبالي مؤخرًا، وتسبب غيابهما في الحد من الفعالية الهجومية، بينما تأثر خط الدفاع بغياب محمد أرنق للإصابة. اقرأ أيضًا الهلال يحقق فوزًا ثمينًا ويطارد صدارة الدوري الرواندي مدرب الهلال السوداني يكشف أزمة قاتلة قبل دوري أبطال أفريقيا وحددت إدارة الهلال السوداني بلوغ نصف نهائي البطولة الأفريقية كطموح أدنى، وسط مهددات حقيقية تواجه الفريق بتراجع فني ملحوظ بالمقارنة مع المستويات التي قدمها بالنسخ الأخيرة من البطولة، مما يضاعف من معاناة المدرب ويضعه تحت مقصلة إقالة مؤكدة في حالة عدم تحقيقه للهدف المنشود. وستحسم مباريات الجولة الأولى من دور المجموعات لدوري أبطال أفريقيا مصير المدرب الألماني، إذ تمثل مواجهتا بيراميدز المصري والمغرب الفاسي اختبارين حقيقيين له؛ فإما الاستمرار في منصبه أو الإقالة حال تعثره في تحقيق نتائج تعزز حظوظ الفريق في بلوغ ربع النهائي. وتأتي هذه التحديات في ظل الحساسية المعهودة في لقاءات الأندية السودانية ونظيرتها المصرية، فضلًا عن الأجواء المشحونة عقب إقصاء حوريا كوناكري الغيني للمريخ، مما زاد من حدة الترقب لمواجهته مع الهلال، في ظل التحديات التي ترافق مبارياتهما ونتائجهما مع الأندية التي تواجههما. من جانبها، قارنت جماهير الهلال السوداني بين أداء الفريق المتواضع في الدوري الرواندي هذا الموسم، وبين انتصاراته الكاسحة ونتائجه القياسية في الموسم الماضي، خاصة في ظل المعاناة التي واجهها في مبارياته الخمس الأولى هذا العام، مما يضاعف من تحديات المدرب جوزيف زينباور بتحقيق لقب شرفي للمسابقة على غرار الموسم الماضي، فضلًا عن الطموح في التقدم لأبعد من محطة ربع النهائي بعد أن توقف عندها بآخر نسختين من دوري أبطال أفريقيا. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق رياضات التنس كرة السلة رياضات ميكانيكية مبارايات اليوم football.summary: يواجه المدرب الألماني جوزيف زينباور تحديات كبيرة مع فريق الهلال السوداني، حيث تراجع مستوى الفريق في الدوري الرواندي هذا الموسم، مما أثار قلق الجماهير. بعد أن كان الهلال قد حقق نجاحات كبيرة في الموسم الماضي، أصبحت النتائج الحالية غير مرضية، مما أدى إلى ضغوط على الإدارة وقد يهدد منصب زينباور في حال استمر تدهور الأداء. يتعين على المدرب تحقيق على الأقل ربع نهائي دوري أبطال أفريقيا، وهو هدف صعب بعد رحيل بعض النجوم وتأثر الفريق بالإصابات. مباريات دور المجموعات القادمة، خاصة ضد بيراميدز المصري والمغرب الفاسي، ستكون حاسمة لمستقبل زينباور، حيث يتوقع الجمهور أداءً أفضل مقارنة بالموسم الماضي. في ظل هذه الظروف، يتطلع الهلال إلى استعادة هيبته وتحقيق نتائج إيجابية تعزز فرصه في المنافسة القارية.

داركو نوفيتش من منصبه مديراً فنياً للفريق الأول لكرة القدم، إلى جانب إنهاء مهام الجهاز الفني المساعد، وذلك ضمن قرارات جديدة تستهدف إعادة ترتيب الأوضاع الفنية والإدارية داخل النادي. وجاء القرار عقب الاجتماع الدوري الخامس لمجلس الإدارة، الذي عُقد عصر اليوم بمكتب رئيس النادي، لمناقشة عدد من الملفات المرتبطة بفريق كرة القدم، ومراجعة الجوانب الفنية والإدارية في إطار مساعي الإدارة لتصحيح المسار وتعزيز الاستقرار. وقرر المجلس تكليف الكابتن جندي نميري بتولي القيادة الفنية للفريق الأول بصورة مؤقتة، كما أعلن إعفاء الجهاز الإداري لكرة القدم من مهامه، مع تكليف المدير الرياضي بترشيح الجهازين الفني والإداري الجديدين بما يتناسب مع متطلبات المرحلة المقبلة وطموحات النادي. وفي سياق إعادة هيكلة العمل داخل قطاع كرة القدم، أعلن مجلس الإدارة تشكيل لجنة مختصة برئاسة رئيس النادي، وعضوية نائب رئيس النادي للشؤون الرياضية نائباً للرئيس، والمدير العام عضواً ومقرراً، والمدير الرياضي، إلى جانب ميرفت حسين الصادق والكابتن فيصل عجب. وأكد مجلس إدارة المريخ أن هذه القرارات تأتي ضمن مراجعة شاملة للأداء الفني والإداري، بهدف معالجة التحديات القائمة، وتعزيز الانضباط والاستقرار، وإعداد الفريق للمرحلة المقبلة وفق رؤية تلبي طموحات جماهير النادي. وشدد المجلس على التزامه باتخاذ الخطوات اللازمة لاستعادة التوازن داخل الفريق، والعمل بروح المسؤولية المؤسسية من أجل مصلحة المريخ وتحقيق تطلعات جماهيره. أقسام الخبر البطولة الدوري السوداني الممتاز النادي المريخ عرض التعليقات المزيد الأخبار المتعلقة المريخ يودّع دوري football.summary: أعلن نادي المريخ السوداني عن إقالة المدرب الصربي داركو نوفيتش من منصبه كمدير فني للفريق الأول لكرة القدم، بالإضافة إلى إنهاء مهام الجهاز الفني المساعد. جاء هذا القرار خلال الاجتماع الدوري الخامس لمجلس الإدارة، الذي عُقد لمناقشة الأوضاع الفنية والإدارية في النادي. تم تكليف الكابتن جندي نميري بقيادة الفريق بشكل مؤقت، كما تم إعفاء الجهاز الإداري لكرة القدم من مهامه. وتهدف هذه القرارات إلى إعادة ترتيب الأوضاع وتعزيز الاستقرار داخل النادي، حيث تم تشكيل لجنة مختصة لمراجعة الأداء الفني والإداري. وأكد المجلس التزامه بتحسين الأداء ومعالجة التحديات القائمة، بهدف تلبية طموحات جماهير المريخ وتحقيق النجاح في المرحلة المقبلة. هذه الخطوات تأتي في إطار سعي الإدارة لاستعادة التوازن وتعزيز الانضباط داخل الفريق.

football.title: مدرب السودان يحظى بدعم هائل قبل موقعتي السنغال - winwin
football.content: مدرب السودان يحظى بدعم هائل قبل موقعتي السنغال مدرب السودان يحظى بدعم هائل قبل موقعتي السنغال مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول مدرب السودان يحظى بدعم هائل قبل موقعتي السنغال جانب من تدريبات لاعبي منتخب السودان (Facebook/ SFA) 8 نوفمبر 2026 مدرب السودان يحظى بدعم هائل قبل موقعتي السنغال السودان السنغال تصفيات كأس الأمم الأفريقية كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' كثف منتخب السودان استعداداته لمواجهتي السنغال الحاسمتين، المقررتين في 12 و16 نوفمبر/ تشرين الثاني الحالي على ملعبي عبد الله واد وجوبا الأولمبي، ضمن الجولتين 3 و4 من منافسات المجموعة العاشرة في تصفيات كأس أمم أفريقيا 2027 . واقتربت صفوف "صقور الجديان" من الاكتمال مع توافد المحترفين في الدوريات الخارجية، إلى مقر المعسكر التحضيري في العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، وتلقى الجهاز الفني دفعة معنوية كبيرة بإنهاء أزمة الثنائي أبو عاقلة عبد الله والجزولي نوح، ليعودا لدعم الفريق في هذين اللقاءين المرتقبين. السودان يواجه السنغال بصفوف مكتملة وصل اللاعب أبوبكر عيسى يوم الأحد 8 نوفمبر تشرين الثاني، ليبدأ تدريباته مع الفريق استعدادًا لمواجهة "أسود التيرانغا"، ملتحقًا بزملائه أبو عاقلة عبد الله والجزولي نوح وأحمد التش بوصولهم فجرًا، بعد غياب الأول والثاني عن مواجهتي إثيوبيا وموزمبيق الماضيتين بسبب أزمة المستحقات. وتعد عودة الثنائي قبل مواجهتي السنغال إضافة نوعية لتعزيز خطي الوسط والهجوم في المنتخب السوداني، لا سيما في ظل غياب سيف الدين مالك بداعي الإصابة. اقرأ أيضًا: أبياه يقف بين الثقة والإقالة قبل موقعة السنغال دفعة مزدوجة لمنتخب السودان قبل موقعة السنغال وتكتمل صفوف منتخب السودان بانضمام نجوم الهلال والمريخ، بعد أن فضل المدرب كواسي أبياه استمرارهم في المنافسة الرسمية، والسماح لهم بخوض مباريات فريقيهما في الدوري الرواندي في ظل توقف البطولات المحلية بالبلاد. وسينضم لاعبو "الأزرق" إلى التدريبات فور فراغهم من التزاماتهم، بينما ينهي لاعبو المريخ
